summary: Outlines an architecture for hosts attached to several networks at once. It introduces the Provisioning Domain, a consistent set of network configuration information, so a host can keep each network's settings separate and choose appropriately. It came from the Multiple Interfaces Architecture Design team.

eli5.summary: If your tablet uses home Wi-Fi and a phone network together, each has its own rules. This keeps each set of rules in its own labeled folder.

questions: how does a device choose which network to use
subtitle: How devices manage multiple networks with separate configurations.

tldr.problem: Devices connected to multiple networks simultaneously receive conflicting configuration (DNS servers, routes, proxies) from different networks, causing applications to fail or behave unexpectedly.
tldr.mechanism: A Provisioning Domain (PvD) groups related network configuration information. PvD-aware devices keep each network's configuration separate and select the appropriate PvD for each connection request.
tldr.outcome: By treating each network's configuration as a distinct domain and choosing PvDs consistently throughout a connection, devices can use multiple networks simultaneously without errors.

facts.label: Configuration elements per PvD
facts.value: Address prefixes, DNS servers, HTTP proxy, DNS suffixes, default gateway

facts.label: Common scenarios
facts.value: 3: mobile with multiple interfaces, VPN connections, ISP with multiple services

today: RFC 7556 is Informational and defines the architecture for managing multiple provisioning domains. It serves as a foundation for companion design documents that specify how DHCP, Router Advertisements, IKEv2, and other protocols convey PvD information to devices.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Nodes (computers, tablets, phones) attached to multiple networks face configuration conflicts. The RFC identifies three categories of problems.

Lack of distinctive management: When a device connects to network A and network B, both may provide DNS server addresses. Without a way to group and name these sets, the device creates a single list mixing servers from both networks. This causes failures when an application tries to resolve a hostname that belongs to one network using a DNS server from the other.

Inappropriate mixed use: An application might try to reach a web proxy provided by network A by looking it up using a DNS server from network B. If the two networks are separate (for example, a company network and a public Wi-Fi hotspot), the proxy address is unreachable.

Use inconsistent with intent: A device might route traffic meant for a VPN through the public network instead, or vice versa. A user might accidentally send corporate traffic through an untrusted network.

The solution is a Provisioning Domain (PvD): a consistent set of network configuration information. A PvD-aware node learns PvD information from networks it attaches to, groups related configuration together, and selects the appropriate PvD for each network operation (name resolution, route selection, opening a listening socket). This keeps configuration from different networks separate and prevents mixed use.
sections.eli5: When a device connects to two networks at once, it gets two sets of configuration (which DNS servers to use, which gateway to talk to, whether to use a proxy). The device must use the right set for each thing it does, not accidentally mix them up.

sections.title: Types of Provisioning Domains
sections.content:
Explicit PvDs are advertised by the network. A network sends PvD information (an identifier and associated configuration) through DHCP options, Router Advertisements, or other mechanisms. A PvD-aware device receives this label and groups the configuration elements that belong to it.

Implicit PvDs are created automatically by a PvD-aware device when networks do not advertise explicit PvD information. By default, configuration from each interface is treated as a separate implicit PvD. This allows PvD-aware devices to provide better behavior than non-PvD-aware devices even in networks that have not been updated to support explicit PvDs.

A single network might advertise multiple explicit PvDs (for example, a service provider offering different packages: best-effort internet, video streaming, VoIP each as a separate PvD). A single interface might have both explicit PvDs (from the network) and implicit PvDs (for unlabeled configuration).

PvDs are not strictly tied to interfaces. Multiple PvDs can exist on one interface, or a single PvD can span multiple interfaces (for example, a home network with multiple internal routers might provide one PvD to all devices regardless of which internal link they use).
sections.eli5: Some networks tell devices 'this is PvD #1 and here is its configuration.' Other networks do not send a label, so the device creates its own label. A network can advertise multiple PvDs if it wants to offer different services, and a device can have multiple PvDs at once.

sections.title: Using PvDs for Network Connections
sections.content:
A PvD-aware node applies PvDs consistently across each network operation.

Name resolution: When an application needs to resolve a domain name, the device selects a PvD (often based on matching a PvD ID or DNS suffix to the name being resolved, or according to a policy). The device performs the name lookup using only the DNS servers configured in that PvD.

Routing and source address: Once the device has a destination IP address, it selects a next-hop router from the appropriate PvD, then selects a source address that belongs to the same PvD.

Listening sockets: When an application opens a listening socket, the operating system applies host policy to determine which PvDs the application is authorized to use. The device binds the socket to an address from one of those PvDs.

Security policy: PvDs themselves do not define security policy, but they enable it. For example, in a VPN scenario, host policy might require that all traffic for a particular application must use the VPN PvD, preventing the application from accidentally leaking information to the public network.
sections.eli5: When a device needs to find a server's address, send data, or listen for incoming connections, it picks one PvD and uses only that PvD's configuration for the whole operation. This prevents accidentally mixing configuration from different networks.

sections.title: Example Scenarios
sections.content:
Mobile node with Wi-Fi and cellular: A phone with cellular and Wi-Fi interfaces may have two implicit PvDs (one per interface) or explicit PvDs if the networks advertise them. The cellular network might send an explicit PvD through the Packet Data Protocol context; the Wi-Fi network might not. The phone automatically creates an implicit PvD for the Wi-Fi configuration.

VPN connection: A device connects to the internet through a home gateway (one PvD) and establishes a VPN tunnel to an enterprise network (second PvD). Routing to addresses within the enterprise range goes through the VPN; routing elsewhere uses the home network. Security policy can restrict applications so they only use the VPN connection.

Service provider with multiple offerings: An ISP might advertise separate PvDs for best-effort internet, video-on-demand, and real-time voice. A home network device automatically learns these PvDs and can use the appropriate one for each service. A set-top box might use one PvD for video, while a PC uses a different PvD for internet browsing.
sections.eli5: A phone gets one PvD from its cellular network and another from Wi-Fi. A laptop might get one PvD for the regular internet and another for an office VPN. A home router might get three PvDs from an ISP: one for internet, one for video, one for phone calls.

sections.title: Implementation and Trust
sections.content:
PvD-aware nodes must not automatically merge configuration from different PvDs, even if one PvD lacks some required element. Merging would recreate the problems the architecture solves. However, a node administrator or application can override this through policy: local configuration can supplement a PvD, or merging can be explicitly allowed for a specific purpose.

PvD identity must be globally unique (to avoid accidental collisions) but uniqueness alone is not enough to prevent attacks. An attacker on an open Wi-Fi network might claim to be the same PvD as an enterprise network, trying to intercept traffic intended for the enterprise.

The RFC defines two types of trust. Untrusted PvDs are those for which no trust relationship exists—implicit PvDs by default, or explicit PvDs from unknown sources. A PvD-aware node must not assume two explicit PvDs with the same identifier are the same unless they are authenticated and authorized.

Trusted PvDs require both authentication (verifying the source) and authorization (confirming that the source is allowed to provide this PvD). Authentication can use cryptographic signatures and certificate chains; authorization can be based on a configured list of trusted PvD identifiers or on the nature of the connection (for example, a mobile phone trusts a PvD from its mobile operator because it received it through authenticated mobile infrastructure).
sections.eli5: A device must not accidentally mix configuration from different PvDs to fix a missing setting. Configuration can come from a network (external) or from the device owner (local). Before trusting a PvD's identity, the device must check a signature or recognize the connection it came from, to prevent attackers from spoofing a PvD.

viz.caption: Without PvDs, configuration mixes; with PvDs, each network's settings stay separate.

left.title: Without PvDs
left.desc: Device receives DNS, routes, proxy settings from both networks in one list. Applications mix settings incorrectly.

right.title: With PvDs
right.desc: Each network's configuration is labeled and kept separate. Device uses the right set for each operation.
